interactions.summary: The reading closes the suicide episode, and Jiang apologizes for moving quickly because the next cantos are crucial to diagnosing what is wrong with Florence.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading followed by Jiang transition

interactions.summary: Canto 14 opens the burning sand of the third ring, where differently stationed souls endure a slow rain of fire.
The reading identifies Capaneus, the blaspheming giant who still defies God under the rain of fire, and has Virgil denounce his unquenched arrogance.
The canto then turns from the burning plain to the red stream and the old man of Crete whose tears generate hell's rivers.

speaker_notes.note: The ASR form 'Copenius' refers to Capaneus, the giant blasphemer of Thebes.

claims.claim: Jiang says the next cantos are especially important because they keep developing the major themes of the poem while trying to explain what is wrong with Florence.
The third ring appears as a barren sand plain where naked souls are distributed by different decrees and punished by a slow rain of fire.
Capaneus is punished more intensely because his arrogance survives death unchanged; even divine torment does not break his defiance.
Virgil identifies the giant as one of the seven kings against Thebes who held and still holds God in disdain.
The old man of Crete allegorically generates hell's rivers through tears that drip from cracks in the metallic body and become Acheron, Styx, Phlegethon, and later Cocytus.

signature_moments.moment: Fire falls on the burning sand like slow snow.
signature_moments.source_phrase: their fall was slow, as snow descends on alps when no wind blows
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most memorable punishment image and sets the emotional texture of the blasphemers' plain.

signature_moments.moment: The blasphemer's own unquenched arrogance is itself the punishment.
signature_moments.source_phrase: No torture other than your own master. Madness could offer pain enough
signature_moments.why_it_matters: Virgil converts punishment from external force into the internal structure of defiant pride.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The giant blasphemer whose defiance of God persists under punishment and exemplifies violence against God.
A metallic allegorical figure whose tears feed the rivers of hell and whose bodily composition encodes civilizational decline.

chronology_notes.note: This packet moves from the suicide wood into Canto 14's blasphemers and then immediately opens the cosmological machinery of hell's rivers.

uncertainty_notes.note: Some place names in the old-man allegory are ASR-rough, but the gold-to-clay body and tear-fed river system are clear.
